questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This stained smear shows bacilli with a 'safety-pin' appearance (arrow). What staining feature produces this look?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bipolar staining (dye concentrates at the two poles of the bacillus)

explanation.summary: Y. pestis characteristically shows bipolar (dye taken up preferentially at each end) staining with stains such as Wright/Giemsa, giving a closed-safety-pin appearance useful in identification.
explanation.whyCorrect: Y. pestis characteristically shows bipolar (dye taken up preferentially at each end) staining with stains such as Wright/Giemsa, giving a closed-safety-pin appearance useful in identification.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This CDC map plots reported human cases concentrated in the western United States. Which zoonotic infection is being mapped?

explanation.summary: Plague is endemic in the rural western US, where rodents, prairie dogs, and their fleas maintain the reservoir; only a handful of human cases (0-17) occur annually, clustered in these western states.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plague is endemic in the rural western US, where rodents, prairie dogs, and their fleas maintain the reservoir; only a handful of human cases (0-17) occur annually, clustered in these western states.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This markedly enlarged, tender lymph node in a febrile patient is the defining lesion of which form of plague?

explanation.summary: A bubo is a massively enlarged, painful regional lymph node draining the site of an infected flea bite; it defines bubonic plague, the most common (80-90%) form of Y. pestis infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: A bubo is a massively enlarged, painful regional lymph node draining the site of an infected flea bite; it defines bubonic plague, the most common (80-90%) form of Y. pestis infection.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This blackened, gangrenous necrosis of the fingers in a septic patient reflects which underlying process that gave plague its 'Black Death' nickname?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Disseminated intravascular coagulation with peripheral ischemic necrosis

explanation.summary: In septicemic plague, systemic inflammation triggers DIC, shock, and microvascular thrombosis, producing acral (fingertip/extremity) ischemic necrosis and gangrene, the classic 'Black Death' appearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: In septicemic plague, systemic inflammation triggers DIC, shock, and microvascular thrombosis, producing acral (fingertip/extremity) ischemic necrosis and gangrene, the classic 'Black Death' appearance.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This map shows US cases of a rabbit-associated zoonosis clustered in the Ozarks. How is this organism usually transmitted to humans?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite of an infected rat flea

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct contact with infected rabbits or bites of ticks and deer flies

explanation.summary: Francisella tularensis (rabbit fever) is transmitted by handling infected rabbits or by arthropod vectors (ticks, deer flies); US cases concentrate in the Ozarks (Missouri and Arkansas).
explanation.whyCorrect: Francisella tularensis (rabbit fever) is transmitted by handling infected rabbits or by arthropod vectors (ticks, deer flies); US cases concentrate in the Ozarks (Missouri and Arkansas).

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This punched-out ulcer at an inoculation site, with regional lymphadenopathy in a rabbit hunter, is characteristic of which condition?

explanation.summary: Ulceroglandular tularemia (75-85% of cases) uniquely ulcerates at the inoculation site along with enlarged local lymph nodes, fever, chills, and malaise, distinguishing it from the non-ulcerating bubo of plague.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ulceroglandular tularemia (75-85% of cases) uniquely ulcerates at the inoculation site along with enlarged local lymph nodes, fever, chills, and malaise, distinguishing it from the non-ulcerating bubo of plague.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: This crusted primary inoculation papule with adjacent lymphadenitis on the neck of a young child with cat exposure is most consistent with which infection?

explanation.summary: A crusted inoculation papule with adjacent regional lymphadenitis in a child who has contact with cats and multiple scratches is the classic presentation of cat scratch disease caused by Bartonella henselae.
explanation.whyCorrect: A crusted inoculation papule with adjacent regional lymphadenitis in a child who has contact with cats and multiple scratches is the classic presentation of cat scratch disease caused by Bartonella henselae.

questions.topicName: Y. pestis, F. tularemia, and B. henselae
questions.stem: These multiple red-purple vascular skin nodules in a severely immunocompromised transplant recipient, caused by a gram-negative bacillus, represent which condition?

explanation.summary: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in severely immunocompromised patients (HIV with low CD4, transplant, chemotherapy) and produces friable, bright red-purple vascular nodules; unlike the histologically similar Kaposi sarcoma, its lesions bleed easily and show neutrophilic infiltrates.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bacillary angiomatosis occurs in severely immunocompromised patients (HIV with low CD4, transplant, chemotherapy) and produces friable, bright red-purple vascular nodules; unlike the histologically similar Kaposi sarcoma, its lesions bleed easily and show neutrophilic infiltrates.
